questions.s: Concerning thalamic relay nuclei:
o: The ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei receive the main output of the globus pallidus internus

The main output of the globus pallidus internus reaches the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei through the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus, which join as the thalamic fasciculus (field H1 of Forel).
These motor thalamic nuclei project to premotor and motor cortex, completing the basal ganglia loop.
The ventral posterior inferior nucleus receives vestibulothalamic fibres

The ventral posterior inferior (VPI) nucleus is the principal thalamic relay for vestibular information, projecting to the vestibular cortex near the postcentral gyrus and insula.
Medial lemniscal and spinothalamic input goes to VPL; trigeminal and taste to VPM.
The centromedian and parafascicular nuclei project chiefly to the cingulate gyrus

The intralaminar centromedian and parafascicular nuclei project heavily to the striatum (and diffusely to cortex).
It is the anterior and lateral dorsal nuclei that project to the cingulate gyrus.
The lateral dorsal nucleus receives fibres from the mammillothalamic tract

The lateral dorsal nucleus receives fibres from the mammillothalamic tract (and the fornix), together with the anterior nucleus. Both project to the cingulate gyrus.
So the lateral dorsal nucleus functions with the anterior group in the limbic (Papez) circuit, despite lying in the lateral group.

questions.s: The ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus:
o: Receives dentatothalamic fibres from the contralateral cerebellum

The ventral lateral nucleus receives dentatothalamic fibres from the contralateral dentate (and interposed) nuclei, crossing in the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles.
This is the cerebellar motor pathway to the cortex.
Receives inputs from the globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata

The ventral lateral nucleus also receives basal ganglia output from the globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata (mostly in its anterior part, overlapping with VA).
The cerebellar and pallidal territories within VL are largely separate.
Projects to the primary motor and supplementary motor cortex

The ventral lateral nucleus projects to the primary motor cortex (area 4) and supplementary and premotor cortex (area 6).
It is a motor relay nucleus.
Is the thalamic target for deep brain stimulation for essential tremor because it receives the medial lemniscus

The ventral intermediate (Vim) part of VL is the target for essential tremor because it receives cerebellar (dentatothalamic) input. The medial lemniscus ends in VPL, just behind it.
Stimulating too far back, in VPL, causes paraesthesiae; too far lateral, in the internal capsule, causes muscle contraction or dysarthria.

questions.s: Regarding the pulvinar and medial dorsal nuclei:
o: The pulvinar has association connections with parietal, temporal and occipital cortex

The pulvinar has extensive association connections with the parietal, temporal and occipital cortex, and with the superior colliculus.
It integrates visual attention and higher-order sensory processing.
The pulvinar is the main relay for the medial lemniscus

The medial lemniscus relays in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus.
The pulvinar is an association nucleus, not a primary sensory relay.
The medial dorsal nucleus projects mainly to the occipital lobe

The medial dorsal (mediodorsal) nucleus projects mainly to the prefrontal cortex, with reciprocal connections, and receives from the amygdala and olfactory regions.
The occipital lobe is connected with the lateral geniculate body and pulvinar.
The medial geniculate body receives the lateral lemniscus via the inferior brachium

The lateral lemniscus ends in the inferior colliculus. The inferior colliculus then projects through the inferior brachium to the medial geniculate body.
So the brachium carries fibres from the colliculus, not the lemniscus itself.

questions.s: Immediately lateral to the ventral intermediate nucleus of the thalamus lies the:
o: Posterior limb of the internal capsule

The posterior limb of the internal capsule lies immediately lateral to the ventral intermediate nucleus of the thalamus.
Current spread from a Vim electrode into the capsule causes contralateral muscle contraction or dysarthria, a key side effect in thalamic deep brain stimulation.
Globus pallidus externus, without intervening white matter

The internal capsule separates the thalamus from the lentiform nucleus (globus pallidus and putamen). There is no direct contact.
The pallidum lies lateral to the posterior limb.
Third ventricle

The third ventricle lies medial to the thalamus, not lateral to it.
From medial to lateral: third ventricle, thalamus, internal capsule, globus pallidus, putamen.
Ventral posterior nucleus, which lies anterior to it

The ventral posterior nucleus lies posterior to the ventral intermediate nucleus, not anterior, and not lateral.
Vim is in the posterior part of VL, directly in front of VPL.

questions.s: Concerning basal ganglia connections:
o: The globus pallidus externus sends GABAergic inhibitory fibres to the subthalamic nucleus

The globus pallidus externus sends GABAergic (inhibitory) fibres to the subthalamic nucleus. This is part of the indirect pathway.
In the indirect pathway, the striatum inhibits GPe, which releases the subthalamic nucleus.
The subthalamic nucleus sends glutamatergic excitatory fibres to the globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata

The subthalamic nucleus sends glutamatergic (excitatory) fibres to the globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata. It is the only excitatory nucleus within the basal ganglia circuit.
Its overactivity in Parkinson's disease is the rationale for subthalamic deep brain stimulation.
The globus pallidus internus excites the thalamus

The outputs of the globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata are GABAergic and tonically inhibit the ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamus.
Movement is released when the striatum (direct pathway) inhibits these output nuclei, so disinhibiting the thalamus.
Nigrostriatal dopamine acting on D1 receptors facilitates the direct pathway

Nigrostriatal dopamine acting on D1 receptors excites the direct pathway striatal neurons. Acting on D2 receptors it inhibits the indirect pathway neurons.
Both effects promote movement, so dopamine loss (Parkinson's disease) reduces movement.

questions.s: The fields of Forel:
o: The lenticular fasciculus (H2) passes through the internal capsule from the globus pallidus internus

The lenticular fasciculus (field H2 of Forel) leaves the globus pallidus internus by passing through the internal capsule, then runs dorsal to the subthalamic nucleus.
It is one of the two pallidothalamic routes.
The ansa lenticularis pierces the posterior limb of the internal capsule

The ansa lenticularis loops around the medial (ventral) edge of the internal capsule rather than piercing it. It is the lenticular fasciculus that passes through the capsule.
"Ansa" means loop: it goes around.
The ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus join to form the thalamic fasciculus (H1)

The ansa lenticularis and the lenticular fasciculus join (in field H of Forel) to form the thalamic fasciculus (H1), which enters the ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamic nuclei.
The thalamic fasciculus also carries cerebellothalamic fibres.
The zona incerta lies between the lenticular fasciculus (H2) and the thalamic fasciculus (H1)

The zona incerta lies between the lenticular fasciculus (H2, ventral) and the thalamic fasciculus (H1, dorsal).
The subthalamic nucleus lies ventral to H2. This layered region is the target area in some deep brain stimulation for tremor.

questions.s: Regarding dopaminergic and other monoaminergic nuclei:
o: The ventral tegmental area supplies dopamine to the ventral striatum and limbic cortex

The ventral tegmental area, medial to the substantia nigra, supplies dopamine to the ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) and limbic and prefrontal cortex: the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways.
These pathways are involved in reward; they are the targets of antipsychotic drugs.
The locus coeruleus is the main noradrenergic nucleus of the brain

The locus coeruleus, in the upper floor of the fourth ventricle near the superior fovea, is the main noradrenergic nucleus of the brain. It is concerned with arousal, attention and fear responses.
Its pigmented neurons give a blue-grey colour in fresh brain.
The raphe nuclei are the main source of serotonin

The raphe nuclei in the midline of the brainstem are the main source of serotonin (5-HT) in the CNS.
They project widely to the forebrain, cerebellum and spinal cord, modulating mood, sleep and pain.
The tuberoinfundibular dopamine pathway from the arcuate nucleus stimulates prolactin release

Dopamine from the arcuate nucleus, carried by the tuberoinfundibular pathway to the portal system, inhibits prolactin release.
So compression of the pituitary stalk (for example by a non-functioning adenoma) raises prolactin through loss of this inhibition (the "stalk effect").

questions.s: Concerning cerebellar corticonuclear projections and lesions:
o: Purkinje cells of the vermis project to the fastigial nucleus

Purkinje cells of the vermis (spinocerebellum) project to the fastigial nucleus.
The intermediate zone projects to the globose and emboliform nuclei, and the lateral hemisphere to the dentate. Medial cortex to medial nucleus.
Purkinje cells of the lateral hemisphere project to the dentate nucleus

Purkinje cells of the lateral hemisphere (cerebrocerebellum) project to the dentate nucleus.
The dentate then projects via the superior peduncle to the contralateral red nucleus and ventral lateral thalamus.
A flocculonodular lesion characteristically produces ipsilateral limb dysmetria

A flocculonodular lesion characteristically produces nystagmus and truncal imbalance (vestibulocerebellar signs).
Ipsilateral limb dysmetria and intention tremor come from lesions of the lateral hemisphere or dentate nucleus.
A midline vermis lesion produces truncal ataxia

A midline vermis lesion produces truncal ataxia with a broad-based gait, as in alcoholic degeneration of the anterior vermis.
Limb coordination tested lying down may be relatively normal.

questions.s: Fibres entering the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle include:
o: Olivocerebellar fibres

Olivocerebellar fibres from the contralateral inferior olive enter through the inferior cerebellar peduncle and end as climbing fibres on Purkinje cells.
They are the largest component of the inferior peduncle.
Cuneocerebellar fibres from the accessory cuneate nucleus

Cuneocerebellar fibres from the accessory cuneate nucleus (upper limb unconscious proprioception) enter through the inferior peduncle, forming the posterior external arcuate fibres.
They are the upper limb counterpart of the posterior spinocerebellar tract.
Posterior spinocerebellar tract

The posterior spinocerebellar tract, from Clarke's column (T1 to L2), enters through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
It carries unconscious proprioception from the lower limb and trunk, ipsilaterally.
Anterior spinocerebellar tract

The anterior spinocerebellar tract ascends to the upper pons and enters the cerebellum through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
It is the classic exception: most cerebellar afferents enter by the inferior or middle peduncles.

questions.s: Regarding hypothalamic nuclei and function:
o: The anterior hypothalamic area promotes heat loss

The anterior hypothalamic area promotes heat loss (sweating, vasodilatation). Its lesions cause hyperthermia.
It acts as the body's "thermostat" for cooling.
The posterior hypothalamus promotes heat conservation

The posterior hypothalamus promotes heat conservation and production (shivering, vasoconstriction). Its lesions cause poikilothermia, where body temperature drifts with the environment.
Anterior = lose heat; posterior = keep heat.
The ventromedial nucleus is a feeding centre whose destruction causes anorexia

The ventromedial nucleus is the satiety centre: its destruction causes hyperphagia and obesity. Lateral hypothalamic lesions cause aphagia (refusal to eat).
Lateral = feeding centre; ventromedial = satiety centre.
The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian pacemaker

The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian pacemaker. It receives direct retinal input through the retinohypothalamic tract, entraining rhythms to light.
It influences melatonin secretion via the pineal.

questions.s: Concerning neuroendocrine control:
o: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone stimulates both TSH and prolactin release

Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates the release of both TSH and prolactin from the anterior pituitary.
That is why primary hypothyroidism, with high TRH, can cause hyperprolactinaemia.
Atrial natriuretic peptide inhibits antidiuretic hormone release

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) inhibits antidiuretic hormone release, opposing its effect and promoting natriuresis and diuresis.
Both are released in response to changes in blood volume.
Oxytocin is produced mainly in the paraventricular nucleus

Last's says oxytocin is produced mainly in the paraventricular nucleus, and vasopressin mainly in the supraoptic nucleus.
Both nuclei make some of each.
Releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary in the hypothalamohypophysial tract

Releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophysial portal veins from the median eminence.
The hypothalamohypophysial nerve tract carries vasopressin and oxytocin to the posterior pituitary.

questions.s: Regarding the central auditory pathway:
o: Auditory information is first represented bilaterally at the superior olivary complex

Auditory information is first represented bilaterally at the superior olivary complex, which receives from both cochlear nuclei.
So a unilateral lesion above the cochlear nuclei does not cause unilateral deafness. One-sided deafness implies a lesion of the ear, nerve or cochlear nucleus.
The anteroventral cochlear nucleus projects to both superior olivary complexes

The anteroventral cochlear nucleus projects to both superior olivary complexes, with fibres crossing in the trapezoid body.
Comparison of timing and loudness between the two ears there allows sound localisation.
The dorsal cochlear nucleus projects through the lateral lemniscus directly to the inferior colliculus

The dorsal cochlear nucleus projects through the contralateral lateral lemniscus directly to the inferior colliculus, bypassing the superior olive.
Its fibres cross in the dorsal acoustic striae.
The primary auditory cortex lies in the posterior transverse temporal gyrus

Last's places the primary auditory cortex (areas 41 and 42) mainly in the anterior transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl, not the posterior one.
The posterior parts of the superior temporal gyrus form the auditory association area (including Wernicke's).

questions.s: The lateral vestibulospinal tract:
o: Arises from the lateral vestibular nucleus (of Deiters)

The lateral vestibulospinal tract arises from the lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters' nucleus).
The medial vestibulospinal tract arises from the medial vestibular nucleus.
Descends ipsilaterally to all levels of the spinal cord

The lateral vestibulospinal tract descends ipsilaterally through the whole length of the cord in the anterior funiculus, facilitating extensor (antigravity) motor neurons.
Unopposed vestibulospinal activity contributes to decerebrate (extensor) rigidity after a lesion between the red and vestibular nuclei.
Is important for posture and balance

Last's says the tract acts mainly on trunk and limb girdle muscles, maintaining posture and balance.
It is driven by the vestibular apparatus and modulated by the cerebellum.
Descends mainly to the cervical cord to control head position

Descent mainly to the cervical cord to control head position describes the medial vestibulospinal tract, from the medial vestibular nucleus, travelling in the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
Lateral = whole cord, posture; medial = neck, head and eye coordination.

questions.s: Concerning the olfactory bulb and cortex:
o: The glomerulus is the basic odorant processing unit of the olfactory bulb

The glomerulus is the basic odorant processing unit of the olfactory bulb. Receptor axons expressing the same receptor converge on a glomerulus and synapse with mitral, tufted and periglomerular cells.
Each glomerulus therefore represents one odorant receptor type.
Periglomerular cells receive direct input from primary olfactory neurones

Periglomerular cells receive direct input from primary olfactory neurons. They are inhibitory interneurons that sharpen the signal between neighbouring glomeruli.
Granule cells provide a second, deeper layer of inhibition.
The piriform cortex includes the uncus and anterior parahippocampal gyrus

The primary olfactory (piriform) cortex includes the uncus and the anterior parahippocampal gyrus, with the cortical amygdala. It mediates conscious perception of smell.
Lesions here can cause olfactory hallucinations (uncinate fits).
Mitral cell axons relay in the medial dorsal thalamic nucleus before reaching the piriform cortex

Mitral cell axons reach the primary olfactory cortex without a thalamic relay. The route through the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus is a secondary pathway to the orbitofrontal cortex.
Olfaction is the only sense whose primary cortex is reached without a thalamic relay.

questions.s: In the Papez circuit:
o: The circuit begins at the subiculum of the hippocampal formation

The Papez circuit begins in the hippocampal formation, with output from the subiculum travelling in the fornix.
The hippocampus receives its input from the entorhinal cortex.
The fornix projects to the medial mammillary nucleus

Most postcommissural fornix fibres end in the medial mammillary nucleus.
Some fornix fibres (precommissural) go to the septal area instead.
The mammillothalamic tract projects to the anterior thalamic nucleus

The mammillothalamic tract projects from the mammillary body to the anterior thalamic nucleus, which projects to the cingulate gyrus.
Lesions of the mammillary bodies or this tract (as in Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome) impair memory.
The cingulum returns impulses to the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus

The cingulum, an association bundle in the cingulate gyrus, carries impulses back to the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus, completing the circuit.
The full loop: hippocampus, fornix, mammillary body, mammillothalamic tract, anterior thalamus, cingulate gyrus, cingulum, entorhinal cortex, hippocampus.

questions.s: Regarding association and commissural tracts:
o: The uncinate fasciculus connects the orbitofrontal cortex with the anterior temporal lobe

The uncinate fasciculus connects the orbitofrontal cortex with the anterior temporal lobe, hooking around the stem of the lateral sulcus.
It links emotional and memory regions of the frontal and temporal lobes.
The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke's area with Broca's area

The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus) with Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus), arching around the posterior end of the lateral sulcus.
Its interruption causes conduction aphasia: fluent speech and good comprehension, but poor repetition.
The hippocampal commissure connects the two fornices

The hippocampal commissure (commissure of the fornix) connects the two crura of the fornix beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum.
It links the two hippocampi.
The posterior commissure contains no fibres related to eye movements

The posterior commissure carries fibres from the pretectal nuclei, the interstitial nucleus of Cajal and the nucleus of Darkschewitsch. These are involved in vertical gaze and the consensual light reflex.
Its compression (for example by a pineal tumour) causes upgaze palsy (Parinaud's syndrome).

questions.s: A lesion of the right medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons (internuclear ophthalmoplegia) produces:
o: Failure of adduction of the right eye on attempted gaze to the left

On gaze to the left, the left abducent nucleus fires; its internuclear neurons cross and ascend in the right MLF to the right medial rectus subnucleus. A right MLF lesion interrupts this, so the right eye fails to adduct.
The internuclear ophthalmoplegia is named for the side of the failed adduction (here, right).
Failure of abduction of the left eye on gaze to the left

Abduction of the left eye on gaze to the left is intact, because the left abducent nucleus and nerve are spared. The abducting eye typically shows nystagmus.
Failure of abduction would mean a VI lesion instead.
Loss of convergence in all cases

Convergence is usually preserved with a pontine MLF lesion, because convergence does not depend on the MLF; it is driven from the midbrain.
Preserved convergence with failed adduction on lateral gaze proves the medial rectus and III are intact.
Paralysis of right lateral rectus

The abducent nucleus and nerve are intact, so right lateral rectus is not paralysed.
An MLF lesion affects only the yoking of the medial rectus to the opposite lateral rectus.

questions.s: Concerning horizontal and vertical gaze centres:
o: The paramedian pontine reticular formation drives the ipsilateral abducent nucleus for horizontal saccades

The paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF), which Last's calls the para-abducent nucleus, drives the ipsilateral abducent nucleus to produce horizontal saccades to the same side.
A PPRF lesion causes an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy.
The rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF lies in the midbrain and generates vertical saccades

The rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF, in the midbrain, generates vertical saccades, working with the interstitial nucleus of Cajal.
Midbrain lesions therefore cause vertical gaze palsies.
The frontal eye field drives saccades to the same side

The frontal eye field drives conjugate gaze to the opposite side. An acute destructive lesion therefore deviates the eyes towards the side of the lesion (the patient "looks at the lesion").
An irritative lesion (seizure) drives the eyes away from the lesion.
Parinaud's syndrome from a pineal tumour includes upgaze palsy and light-near dissociation

Parinaud's (dorsal midbrain) syndrome, classically from a pineal tumour compressing the pretectum and posterior commissure, includes upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation of the pupils, convergence-retraction nystagmus and lid retraction.
The pupils react to accommodation but not to light.

questions.s: Match the brainstem vascular syndromes:
o: Weber's syndrome: ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiplegia

Weber's syndrome is a ventral midbrain lesion affecting the fascicles of III and the cerebral peduncle: ipsilateral III palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.
It is typically caused by occlusion of paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery.
Benedikt's syndrome: ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral tremor or ataxia

Benedikt's syndrome is a tegmental midbrain lesion involving III fascicles and the red nucleus: ipsilateral III palsy with contralateral tremor or ataxia.
The red nucleus and dentatothalamic fibres are damaged after they cross.
Millard-Gubler syndrome: ipsilateral abducent and facial palsy with contralateral hemiplegia

Millard–Gubler syndrome is a ventral caudal pontine lesion: ipsilateral VI and VII palsy with contralateral hemiplegia (corticospinal fibres above their decussation).
A "crossed" pattern like this localises the lesion to the brainstem.
AICA occlusion: ipsilateral deafness and facial weakness with Horner's syndrome

AICA occlusion (lateral inferior pontine syndrome) causes ipsilateral deafness (labyrinthine artery, usually from AICA), facial weakness, Horner's syndrome and limb ataxia, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature.
Deafness distinguishes it from the lateral medullary (PICA) syndrome.

questions.s: Occlusion of a single artery of Percheron causes:
o: Bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction

The artery of Percheron is a single trunk from one P1 segment that supplies the paramedian parts of both thalami (and often the rostral midbrain). Its occlusion causes bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction.
Normally each side has its own thalamoperforating arteries.
Altered consciousness and vertical gaze palsy

Bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction causes altered consciousness (the intralaminar nuclei) and, if the rostral midbrain is involved, vertical gaze palsy.
Memory disturbance is also common.
A characteristic dense contralateral hemiplegia as the main sign

Motor weakness is not the main feature. Somnolence, memory loss and vertical gaze disturbance dominate.
A dense hemiplegia would suggest involvement of the internal capsule or cerebral peduncle instead.
Infarction in a territory supplied from the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery

The thalamoperforating (paramedian) arteries, including the artery of Percheron, arise from the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery, before the posterior communicating junction.
So aneurysms or surgery at the basilar tip put them at risk.

questions.s: Regarding the trigeminal sensory system:
o: The spinal nucleus has subnuclei oralis, interpolaris and caudalis

The spinal trigeminal nucleus has three subnuclei: oralis (fine orofacial touch), interpolaris (touch and dental pain) and caudalis (pain and temperature).
Caudalis is continuous with the substantia gelatinosa of the upper cord.
Pain from the face follows an onion-skin pattern in the spinal nucleus

Last's describes an onion-skin pattern in the spinal nucleus: perioral areas are represented rostrally, and more peripheral rings of the face progressively caudally.
A lesion of the lower spinal nucleus therefore causes sensory loss on the outer face, sparing the area around the mouth.
Second-order fibres from the main sensory nucleus project to the contralateral VPM

Second-order fibres from the main sensory nucleus project mainly to the contralateral VPM through the trigeminal lemniscus, with some uncrossed dorsal fibres.
The face is thus represented mainly in the opposite thalamus and cortex, like the body.
The mesencephalic nucleus projects mainly to the ipsilateral VPL

Mesencephalic neurons are primary afferents. They mediate the jaw jerk through the motor nucleus and do not project to the thalamus in this way. Facial sensation relays in VPM, not VPL.
VPL serves the body (medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tracts).

questions.s: Concerning the choroidal fissure of the lateral ventricle:
o: It lies between the fornix and the thalamus

In the body of the lateral ventricle the choroidal fissure lies between the fornix and the thalamus. In the temporal horn it lies between the fimbria and the stria terminalis.
The choroid plexus is attached along this fissure.
Its anterior limit is the interventricular foramen

The choroidal fissure begins at the interventricular foramen and curves back and down into the inferior horn.
Its C-shape follows the fornix.
The anterior choroidal artery enters its inferior end at the temporal horn

The anterior choroidal artery enters the inferior end of the choroidal fissure in the temporal horn, just above the uncus (the inferior choroidal point).
This point is a landmark in temporal lobe surgery.
The septal vein runs through it to the vein of Galen

The septal veins run on the septum pellucidum to join the internal cerebral vein near the interventricular foramen. They do not run through the choroidal fissure.
The thalamostriate vein runs in the groove between caudate and thalamus to the same point.

questions.s: Regarding the anterior choroidal artery territory (neurosurgical texts):
o: It includes the posterior limb of the internal capsule

The territory of the anterior choroidal artery includes the lower part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
That is why its occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia.
It includes the medial globus pallidus

Rhoton-based neurosurgical sources include the medial globus pallidus in the anterior choroidal territory.
This territory is variable and overlaps with lenticulostriate branches.
It includes the lateral geniculate body and optic tract

The anterior choroidal artery supplies the optic tract and lateral geniculate body. Infarction gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
The full syndrome is hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and hemianopia.
Its usual origin is the cavernous internal carotid artery

The anterior choroidal artery arises from the supraclinoid (communicating) segment of the internal carotid artery, distal to the posterior communicating artery.
The cavernous segment gives the meningohypophyseal and inferolateral trunks instead.

questions.s: Concerning spinal cord lamination and syndromes:
o: In the anterolateral tract sacral fibres lie most superficially

Last's says in the anterolateral (spinothalamic) tract sacral fibres lie most superficially (laterally), with cervical fibres deepest.
So intramedullary lesions, expanding from the centre, may spare sacral sensation (sacral sparing).
In the posterior columns cervical fibres lie most medially

In the posterior columns sacral fibres lie most medially. Cervical fibres are added laterally as the columns ascend.
This is the reverse of the spinothalamic and lateral corticospinal tracts.
Central cord syndrome affects the upper limbs more than the lower limbs

Central cord syndrome affects the upper limbs more than the lower limbs. Last's explains this by the more lateral position of lumbar and sacral corticospinal fibres, away from a central lesion.
It typically follows hyperextension injury of a stenotic cervical spine.
The anterior spinal artery syndrome abolishes vibration sense

The posterior columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, so they are spared in anterior spinal artery syndrome. Vibration and proprioception remain.
Paralysis and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion are the features.
